brief.notification_title: Relief bounce into Fed week; Brent dip mostly roll
brief.market_summary: US stocks are up about 0.7% at 10:39 ET (S&P 7,677, Nasdaq +0.78%, SMH +1.54%, VIX 18.25). The lift comes from oil easing on Saudi–Iran talks and from Anthropic's S-1 lifting AI names. Treasuries are adding to last week's rally: the 10Y is at 4.966% (−2.2bp today, −17bp on the week) and the 30Y at 5.286%. That happened while the Fed is still in a hiking cycle, which makes it a flight to quality, not a dovish signal. Brent's screen price of $109.97 (−5.8%) is mostly the switch to the January contract. December Brent traded around $114.4–115.9, down roughly 1–2%, and BNO is −2.1%. Crypto lags: BTC is $79,806, just under $80K, and ETH is $2,312. Most alt L1s are down 4–10% on the week.
brief.since_last:
- **Verizon beat and raised:** adj. EPS $1.31 vs $1.27, a third straight guidance raise.
- **Anthropic S-1 is public:** H1 revenue $16.3B, Nasdaq ticker ANT (n25). It is lifting chips.
- **Meta stock offering:** Meta plans to raise up to $95B through a stock offering to fund AI (n20). That is a large new supply of shares.
- **Musk on neoclouds:** his "guppy-level death" comment hit neocloud stocks; CRWV −5% (n29).
- **Iran and Saudi:** the Saudi defence minister is in Tehran for de-escalation talks (n41). Houthis claimed hits on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, the main export route that bypasses Hormuz (n130). Trump says it is "decision time" on Iran (n1).
- **Brazil:** Lula was re-elected and Brazilian assets crashed (EWZ about −26% pre-market) (n19).
- **Strategy** bought no BTC last week and spent $205M on STRC buybacks instead (n44).
- **Brent contract roll:** front-month Brent rolled from December to January.
- **No triggers hit:** none of last brief's invalidation levels were reached.

The second-lowest final reading on record, while inflation expectations are still rising. That is the stagflation mix that keeps the Fed leaning toward a hike even as consumers weaken.
A low-impact release. I don't have the actual, so I'm not reading anything into it.
A miss would add to the weak-consumer story after UMich. That would support the bond rally and hurt discretionary stocks (XLY +1.7% today).

94 of 100 economists expect a hold; CME prices about 10% odds of a hike. A December hike is already largely expected, so the question is whether Warsh confirms it (n166). Hawkish confirmation means bills keep their yield and the long end may rally further on growth fears. Any opening to cuts would trigger the prior brief's rule to rotate part of SGOV into IEF.
My sources disagree on the consensus and the prior, so I'm treating anything near 3% as in line. A strong number alongside hot PCE would push yields back up after last week's 17bp fall.
This is the week's key inflation print, and it lands the day after the Fed. A 0.4% would lock in December and likely hit duration and growth stocks. A 0.2% would let the bond rally run.
A softer reading would ease wage-spiral worries. It matters less than PCE unless it surprises at 1% or higher.

sections.summary: A relief rally after Friday's −0.5%: S&P +0.70%, Nasdaq +0.78%, SMH +1.54%, helped by softer oil and the Anthropic filing (n5, n10). Under the surface, AI funding stress keeps growing. Meta is raising up to $95B in stock (n20), Musk is warning on neoclouds (n29), and 6 of the 10 largest S&P names fell last week (n94). Breadth has rotated toward defensives and value: XLV +5.7% and XLP +7.7% over 1M, versus SMH −11.7%.
key_points: Q3 season so far (FactSet, 24% reported): 83% beat on EPS, but only 2.1% above estimates in aggregate vs a 7.5% five-year average. Beats are small.
Brazil shock: Lula re-elected; EWZ about −26% pre-market, NU −21%, MELI −10% (n19). This looks country-specific; I don't see contagion to the US yet.
Deals: EQT is buying Range Resources (RRC +15%), and Surgery Partners jumped on reports of a $6B takeover.

sections.summary: Long yields keep falling even though the Fed is in a hiking cycle and a December hike is largely priced (n107, n159). The 10Y is at 4.966% and the 30Y at 5.286%, down 17–19bp on the week. That is a quality bid out of stocks and AI credit, not a bet on cuts (n168, n135). Bills still yield about 4.0–4.2%. The week's supply (2y, 5y, 7y auctions) and Thursday's PCE are the near-term tests.
key_points: Market yields: 13-week bill 4.04%, 5Y 4.80%, 10Y 4.97%, 30Y 5.29%. Official curve on Fri 10/23: 2s10s +31bp, 3m10y +78bp.
On the week, TLT +3.05% and IEF +1.29%, but HYG is −0.73% over 1M vs LQD +1.07%. Credit prefers quality, which confirms the risk-off undertone.
Auctions: 2y $69B today (last 4.787%), 5y $70B Tue (last about 5.03%), 7y $44B Thu (last about 5.09%).
Fed: about 10% odds of a hike Wednesday; the focus is on Warsh's December guidance (n166). Zandi calls a hike a 'misstep' (n49).

sections.summary: December Brent eased to about $114.4–115.9, down roughly 1–2% from Friday's $116.72 six-month-high settle. The drop came on Saudi–Iran talks in Tehran (n41). The −5.8% on the screen is mostly the roll to January, which trades around $110. Supply risk hasn't gone away: Houthis claimed hits on the East-West pipeline (n130), and Trump says a deal-or-strike decision is near (n1). Meanwhile Saudi output has recovered to 8M bpd (n92) and Iraqi exports are back to pre-war levels (n118).
key_points: The roughly $4 gap between December and January is steep backwardation: the market expects supply to normalise.
WTI $100.85 (−2.3%), BNO $69.49 (−2.1%). BNO's −2.1% is the real move, not BZ=F's −5.8%.
IEA's Birol sees no path back to pre-war prices in 2027 (n40). European gas is at a four-year high (n173).
OPEC+ meets 1 Nov; API and EIA inventories come Tue and Wed. Trump has floated resuming strikes after the 3 Nov midterms.

brief.instructor_take: I'd treat today's bounce as relief, not resolution. The week stacks binary events: FOMC Wednesday, Microsoft and Alphabet that night, PCE, GDP and Amazon Thursday, Exxon and Chevron Friday, then the midterms and Trump's Iran decision. Prices on a Monday tell you little about where that lands. The signal I'd focus on is in bonds. The 10Y fell 17bp in a week while the Fed is hiking, HYG lagged LQD, and Meta needs $95B of new stock to fund AI. Together that says money is leaving the AI-capex trade for safety, and a 0.7% green day doesn't change that. A less experienced investor might also see Brent −5.8% and think the oil story broke. Most of that is the contract roll; the real move is BNO's −2.1%, and Saudi pipeline attacks are still happening. My positioning: new cash stays in T-bills at about 4%, oil exposure comes through producers whose Q3 earnings are roughly double last year's, and I don't chase the semis bounce before the hyperscalers report capex. Two things would change my mind: Microsoft and Alphabet beating and raising with capex returns investors accept, plus a 0.2% core PCE. Then I'd move cash into equities and duration rather than bills. The other is a credible Iran deal; I'd then cut XLE fast.

top_ideas.title: Keep dry powder in T-bills through Fed and PCE
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep new cash in T-bills until the Fed, PCE and megacap prints pass
top_ideas.thesis: Bills pay about 4.0–4.2% and gain if the Fed confirms a December hike. Any cash earmarked for new positions earns that while the week's binary events play out. Last week's 17bp rally in the 10Y already used up much of the easy duration gain, so I'd rather keep the option to buy later.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start from the policy path. The Fed hiked in September, a December hike is largely priced, and Thursday's core PCE is expected to rise to 0.3% from 0.2%, with UMich inflation expectations at 4.7%. In that setting a T-bill reprices upward with each hike, so the front end pays me to wait. The trap is chasing the long-end rally: the 10Y fell to 4.97% on a safe-haven bid, not on cuts. A hot PCE or a 3%+ GDP print plus $183B of 2y, 5y and 7y supply this week could easily push it back above 5%. I prefer SGOV to SHY because it carries essentially no duration risk, and to IEF because I don't yet know if the bond rally is a growth scare or a blip. My rule is unchanged from yesterday. If the Fed or Warsh opens the door to cuts, I move a third into IEF. If the 10Y closes above 5.15% after PCE, I start scaling into IEF at the better yield. I'd be wrong in the opportunity-cost sense if the AI-credit stress deepens and the 10Y drops toward 4.75%; I accept that risk for the flexibility.

top_ideas.title: Own the oil shock through producers, not futures
top_ideas.one_liner: Own $110 oil via XLE: half in, add near $67 or after XOM/CVX
top_ideas.thesis: Brent above $110 is roughly doubling producer earnings (XOM est $3.90 vs $1.88, CVX $4.78 vs $1.85), and SLB just signalled a stronger 2027. XLE gives that cash flow without the roll and headline risk of futures. Today's 0.5% dip met the entry rule.
top_ideas.reasoning: Today's lesson explains why I want producers rather than BNO. The Brent curve is steeply backwardated, January about $4 below December. The market is telling you it expects supply to normalise, and Saudi output at 8M bpd and Iraqi exports back to pre-war levels support that. A futures holder is betting spot stays high. A producer only needs prices to stay well above its costs long enough to bank a few huge quarters, which it will at $100+. The evidence is solid: SLB beat and guided 2027 higher, PSX is expected to earn about $12 vs $2.52, and XOM and CVX report Friday. XLE opened at about $69, below the $70.50 trigger, so the first half is in. I'd add the second half on a dip to about $67 or after strong Friday reports, not into a headline spike. What changes my mind is a real de-escalation: the Tehran talks producing a framework, or Trump choosing a deal. That could take $10–15 off Brent quickly, which is why the stop is firm.

top_ideas.title: Stay out of ETH and alt L1s until flows turn
top_ideas.one_liner: Still avoid ETH: 4th week of ETF outflows, no buyer in sight
top_ideas.thesis: ETH is down 14.6% over a month vs BTC's 5.4%. ETF outflows hit a fourth week (about −$1.18B in October), and the Glamsterdam upgrade has slipped. With FOMC, PCE and a large options expiry this week, there's no reason to catch this.
top_ideas.reasoning: Over the past month BTC is −5.4%, ETH −14.6%, and SUI, ADA and AVAX −18% to −23%. When the major falls slowly and everything further out on the risk curve falls two to four times faster, the market is shrinking risk, not rotating. Look at the marginal buyer. ETH ETFs have had four straight weekly outflows, mostly from BlackRock's ETHA. The Coinbase premium has been negative for 33 days, and Strategy, a reliable BTC buyer, paused purchases (n44). Galaxy's call that the bear market is over (n68) is an opinion; flows are evidence, and the flows still say no. I'm calling this avoid, not sell, because the investor profile can't short and ETH could bounce hard if the Fed and megacaps go well. If you hold ETH or alt L1s, use bounces toward $2,500 to trim, and don't average down. I'd change my mind if ETH reclaims $2,700 with three or more straight days of net spot ETF inflows. That would mean institutional demand is back.

lesson.explanation: Oil futures expire monthly. Price feeds that show a 'continuous' contract (like BZ=F) jump from the expiring month to the next one on roll day. When the curve is in backwardation, near months cost more than later ones, so that jump looks like a price drop nobody actually suffered. Backwardation also carries information: buyers pay up for barrels now and expect supply to loosen later. That matters for whether you hold futures funds, which depend on the curve, or producers, whose earnings depend on prices staying above their costs.
lesson.todays_example: BZ=F shows Brent at $109.97, −5.78%. But December Brent traded around $114.4–115.9 (down about 1–2%), and January was about $110.44 vs $111.70 prior. BNO's −2.11% is the real P&L. The roughly $4 December–January gap is why I own XLE instead of betting on spot staying above $115.
